newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-Australia's budget fails to win over markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Australia's budget fails to win over markets.

text.p: Australia's conservative government unveiled a cautious mid-term budget on Tuesday, disappointing financial markets with modest spending cuts and offering voters only a minor tax break.

Treasurer Peter Costello projected a higher-than-expected underlying deficit, which excludes windfalls such as asset sales, of A$3.85 billion for the year from July, down from A$6.86 billion in 1996/97.
Costello said his second budget would improve the climate for business, boost economic growth and help combat the stubborn jobless rate.
"The budget I have brought down tonight takes us further down the path which will build a future of opportunity for Australia," Costello told parliament.

But financial markets reacted badly. The Australian dollar quickly lost half a cent to 77.75 U.S. cents and bonds were also marked down. Fund managers said the budget would be neutral-to-weaker for the local share market.
"The market was hoping for a memorable event, but all it got was a forgettable budget," said Steve Shuster, head of foreign exchange at Citibank Australia.
Budget cuts amounted to just A$352 million, well down on market forecasts of up to A$1.5 billion, and economists had expected the deficit to be pared back to about A$2 billion.
But Costello said the cuts would be enough to achieve an underlying surplus of A$1.597 billion in 1998/99, the first since 1990/91, and well ahead of the targetted budget balance.
The biggest carrot was a 15-percent tax rebate on savings interest, targetted at the government's middle Australia constituency.
But that scheme, to cost A$350 million in the first year, will not kick in until 1998/99, just ahead of the next election due in early 1999. It was also less than previously promised.
The budget forecast accelerating but modest economic growth of 3.75 percent and continuing low inflation of one percent.

But there was little joy for the unemployed. Although a work for welfare scheme will be implemented to help the jobless gain work skills, the unemployment rate is tipped to fall only marginally to 8.25 percent, year-average, from 8.75 percent.

Costello said the government had met its promise of turning Australia's finances around from deficit to surplus in its first term. He said the budget would be welcomed by the central bank and help put a ceiling on interest rates.

"The story on the economy is a good one -- we're forecasting a pick-up in growth, a pick-up in employment ... and very favourable prospects not just I think for this year, but for the years ahead," he told reporters.
"Australia is now paying its way again. This is a very good effort by world standards."
Economists generally accepted that the country's finances were in good shape, but said Costello should have done more to exploit that.
"The economic forecasts are a tad conservative and as a result the outcomes are a bit less than what we were expecting," said Hans Kunnen, economist at Colonial State Bank.
"If you forecast lower economic growth, you get less tax revenue and you get a bigger budget deficit than what you might have otherwise got. So that was a bit disappointing."
With asset sales and other one-off items, the budget's bottom line for 1997/98 will be a surplus of A$6.42 billion, or 1.2 percent of gross domestic product.
The budget carried some pain -- notably higher medicine costs and a little-improved outlook for unemployment -- but was unlikely to spook voters.

Prime Minister John Howard had looked to the budget to help halt a slide in the government's opinion polls rating, distract voters from a divisive land rights row and check the surging popularity of right-wing politician Pauline Hason.

A newspaper poll published earlier on Tuesday showed the government's support at 40 percent, just one point ahead of the Labor opposition and compared with a steady 12-point lead for most of the past 14 months since the last election.
Hanson's newly-formed One Nation Party increased two points over the past week to nine percent -- five points ahead of the traditional third political force, the Australian Democrats.
